By Abhishek Vishnoi and Winnie HsuNovember 1, 2026 at 12:00 AM UTCBookmark
Save
Takeaways by Bloomberg AI
Asia’s AI-heavy stock markets face a new US policy wildcard in the midterm elections, with the outcome potentially reshaping the tech trade and sectors from clean energy to defense.
A Democratic sweep of both chambers of Congress would likely bring greater scrutiny of the AI industry and data-center buildout. An unexpected Republican hold would offer more policy continuity, potentially benefiting Korean and Taiwanese chipmakers and other suppliers to the US technology boom, according to strategists. Currently, polls and prediction markets indicate a high likelihood that Republicans will lose control of the House of Representatives, while the outcome for the Senate is less certain.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan appointed Muhsin Atci, head of the nation’s tax inspection board, as chief of Turkey’s market regulator to help deal with an investment fund crisis that rocked financial markets.
Erdogan also appointed Ersin Basar Ekmekci as the Capital Markets Board’s deputy chairman and Yasemin Girici as a member, according to an official gazette item published early Sunday.

Senegalese lawmakers have again rejected the government’s revised 2026 finance law, prolonging a standoff that threatens to delay approval of a crucial International Monetary Fund program.
The parliament’s Finance and Budgetary Control Committee remained divided after talks late Friday over the treatment of special funds and assistance for vulnerable households, according to lawmakers and a government official involved in the discussions.

Takeaways by Bloomberg AI
With control of Congress hanging on a number of razor-thin races, both Democrats and Republicans are seizing on voters’ frustrations with rising credit card debt to win over inflation-weary Americans.
Credit card interest rates are now over 20% on average — nearly double what they were a decade ago — compounding the burden of monthly payments. The mix of high rates, a pickup in inflation and rising costs across the broader economy has helped drive the credit card delinquency rate toward its highest level since 2011.

Takeaways by Bloomberg AI
Vladimir Putin’s possible attendance at the Group of 20 leaders’ summit in Florida in December would risk regularizing Russia’s return to international forums while its war in Ukraine continues, according to the European Union’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas.
The US invitation to the Russian leader “poses a lot of big questions,” Kallas said on Saturday in an interview with Bloomberg Television. It risks “normalizing the war crimes being committed every day now” in Ukraine, she added.

Speaking with host Lisa Mateo, Graham says newer venues are dedicating more restroom capacity to women, while upgrades at older stadiums can carry significant costs.

Haunted Attractions Help Revive Neighborhoods
Journalist Elizabeth Yuko tells Bloomberg This Weekend how haunted attractions are drawing visitors and investment to struggling neighborhoods, including Baltimore’s Old Town and former industrial districts in Kansas City and Salt Lake City. Speaking with hosts David Gura and Lisa Mateo, Yuko explains how haunted-house operators can become unlikely partners in urban revitalization by investing in infrastructure, attracting businesses and finding new uses for neglected properties.

item.title: EU Foreign Policy Chief Warns Against Normalizing Russia
item.description: EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas tells Bloomberg This Weekend that Russia is escalating its war in Ukraine and is not serious about peace, criticizing Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov’s statements at the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta and warning against normalizing Moscow on the international stage. Speaking with host David Gura, Kallas also calls for a diplomatic solution to tensions with Iran and discusses efforts to deepen the EU’s relationship with Canada through greater cooperation on trade, energy and defense. (Source: Bloomberg)
